perf(search): Load result rows with one query

The search page ran one query per result row, which is the N+1 problem.
At the 95th percentile the page took 2.4 seconds. load() now fetches all
requested items in one query with `any(%s)`. That brings the 95th
percentile to about 300 ms.

The result changes in two ways. Rows come back in database order, not in
the order of ids. Ids without a matching row are left out, where the old
code put None in their place.

perf(search): Fetch result rows in one query

The search page took 2.4 seconds at the 95th percentile. It ran one
query for each result row, so the number of database round trips grew
with the number of results.

load now fetches all rows with one query that matches the ids with
`any`. The search page takes about 300 ms at the 95th percentile. The
rows come back in database order, not in the order of the ids.

perf(search): Load result rows with one query

The search page ran one query per result row, which is the N+1 problem.
At the 95th percentile the page took 2.4 seconds. load() now fetches
all rows for the given ids in one query, using `id = any(...)`. At the
95th percentile the page now takes about 300 ms.

The new query does not return rows in the order of ids, and it skips
ids that have no matching row. The old loop returned None for a missing
id. Callers that depend on order or on None entries must handle that.

perf(search): Load result rows in one query

The search page ran one query for each result row. This is the N+1
problem: the page made a round trip to the database for every row it
showed, so its latency grew with the number of results. At the 95th
percentile, the page took 2.4 seconds.

Load all rows with one query that uses `id = any(...)`. The 95th
percentile drops to about 300 ms.

The query has no ORDER BY, so rows come back in database order, not
in the order of the given ids. It also returns no row for an id that
does not exist.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Haiku 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(search): Load result rows with one query

The search page ran one query for each result row. This is the N+1
query problem: a page cost one database round trip per row, and the
95th percentile response time reached 2.4 seconds.

Load all rows for the result ids in one query instead. The page now
reaches about 300 ms at the 95th percentile.

The result no longer keeps the order of the ids, and ids without a
matching row are left out. The old loop returned one entry per id.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Haiku 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(search): Load result rows in one query

The search page ran one query per result row, which is the N+1 query
problem. At the 95th percentile the page took 2.4 seconds. load() now
fetches all rows with a single query that matches `id = any(...)`. With
this change the page takes about 300 ms at the 95th percentile.

load() no longer returns None for ids that have no matching row, and
the returned rows do not follow the order of ids. Callers that relied on
